prompt: What is Linux's actual relationship to Unix?
hint: Ask what was copied: the code, or the way it behaves.

choices.text: A fork of the Unix source code, taken in 1991
choices.why: No Unix code was taken. That is exactly what could not be done, and the reason the kernel was written from nothing.

choices.text: A reimplementation that copied the interface and none of the code
choices.why: Written from scratch to behave like Unix, which is why it is legally free of it and compatible with it anyway.

choices.text: The same thing under a different name, after the trademark changed hands
choices.why: UNIX is a live trademark with a certification behind it, and Linux does not hold it.

choices.text: A later version of Unix, released by Bell Labs
choices.why: Bell Labs had nothing to do with it. Linux began as one person's project in Helsinki.

prompt: You learn a command on Linux and run it on macOS. POSIX means you can safely assume:
hint: POSIX is a floor. Think about which half of a command line it describes.

choices.text: Very little; the resemblance between the two is superficial
choices.why: Too pessimistic. macOS is a registered UNIX and the core commands genuinely are the same.

choices.text: The command, its flags and the exact text it prints are identical everywhere
choices.why: Output formats and extra flags are precisely where GNU and BSD tools diverge.

choices.text: Whatever runs on one will run unchanged on the other
choices.why: Package managers, service managers and `/proc` have no equivalent, and none of them is POSIX.

choices.text: The command exists and does the same job, though some flags differ
choices.why: The standard fixes the names and the core behaviour, and leaves the extensions above it to each system.

prompt: Which of these carry from a Linux machine to a Mac's Terminal? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate the agreement from what each system built on top of it.

choices.text: `|` sending one program's output into the next
choices.why: Pipes are in the standard and work identically.

choices.text: Paths starting at `/`, with no drive letters
choices.why: One rooted tree is part of the agreement.

choices.text: `apt install` for adding software
choices.why: Package management is not POSIX. macOS has no `apt`.

choices.text: Owner, group and other permission bits
choices.why: The permission model is in the standard.

choices.text: `systemctl` for starting and stopping services
choices.why: systemd is Linux's, and not even every Linux has it. macOS uses launchd.

choices.text: Reading process information out of `/proc`
choices.why: `/proc` is a Linux invention. macOS has no such directory.

prompt: Fill the blank: on Ubuntu, `/bin/sh` is not bash — it is a symbolic link to ___, a smaller and stricter shell.
hint: The section shows the `ls -l` output that says so.

prompt: Match each system to where it actually comes from.
hint: Two of them share an ancestor, one imitated it, and one never met it.

pairs.right: Written from nothing to behave like Unix, sharing no code with it
Descends from BSD, and is a formally registered UNIX
A separate lineage out of VMS, with no Unix ancestry at all
A direct continuation of the Berkeley line

right_distractors: A rewrite of System V commissioned by Bell Labs in the 1980s
A Linux distribution with the kernel replaced

prompt: You type `dcoker ps` and get back `bash: dcoker: command not found`. Which layer is speaking?
hint: The message names itself before the colon.

choices.text: The shell
choices.why: It looked for a program with that name, found none, and said so — and it signed the message `bash:`.

choices.text: The kernel
choices.why: The kernel was never asked. Nothing got as far as being run.

choices.text: Docker, reporting that it did not recognise the subcommand
choices.why: Docker was never reached — and that is the point of reading the prefix.

choices.text: The terminal emulator
choices.why: The terminal drew those characters and has no idea what they mean.

prompt: You run `tty` and it prints `/dev/pts/0`. What is that?
hint: The name is a museum piece. What was a terminal, originally?

choices.text: The file your command's output is being written to
choices.why: Output flows through it, but it is a device rather than a file somebody would open later.

choices.text: A temporary directory the shell uses while it runs
choices.why: Nothing under `/dev` is a scratch directory. It is where devices appear.

choices.text: A pseudo-terminal: the software stand-in for a keyboard and screen
choices.why: Your shell believes it is talking to hardware; it is talking to a window pretending to be some.

choices.text: The physical serial port your terminal is connected to, at the other end of a cable
choices.why: That would be `/dev/ttyS0`. The `pts` form exists precisely because there is no cable.

prompt: You type `zsh` and get a zsh prompt. Now `echo $0` prints `zsh` and `echo $SHELL` prints `/bin/bash`. Why do they disagree?
hint: The two variables answer two different questions.

choices.text: `$SHELL` is stale and will correct itself at the next command
choices.why: It is not stale. It is answering a different question, correctly.

choices.text: One of them reads the full path while the other reads the short name of the very same shell
choices.why: They name two different shells here, not one shell written two ways.

choices.text: zsh failed to start, so bash is still the shell you are typing into
choices.why: `$0` saying `zsh` is the evidence that it did start.

choices.text: `$0` is the shell running now; `$SHELL` is your account's login shell
choices.why: Starting a shell by hand changes what is running and changes nothing about your account.

prompt: Match each symptom to the layer responsible for it.
hint: Ask who would have had to be asked before that message could exist.

pairs.right: The shell — it searched and found no such program
The kernel — it was asked, and it refused

pairs.left: Text in the wrong place, colours stuck on
pairs.right: The terminal emulator — the drawing is confused, not the command

pairs.left: No new prompt, nothing printed, nothing wrong
pairs.right: The program — it is still running and has not finished

right_distractors: The network — the machine has lost its connection
The disk — the filesystem is full and cannot be written to

prompt: Put the shell's loop in order, from the moment you press enter.
items: Expand what you wrote — `*` becomes a list of files, `$HOME` becomes a path
Ask the kernel to run it
trap: The common mistake is putting the expansion after the program is found. It happens first, and that is why `rm *.txt` hands `rm` a list of filenames rather than a `*`.

prompt: Which of these are true of the shell? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section's claim is that it is more ordinary than it looks.

choices.text: It is an ordinary program, with a name and a file
choices.why: Exactly as ordinary as `ls`. Its job just happens to be starting other programs.

choices.text: You can replace it with a different one
choices.why: bash, zsh, dash, fish — the choice is yours and the system does not mind.

choices.text: It is part of the Linux kernel
choices.why: The kernel is the one program in the middle. The shell came from elsewhere entirely.

choices.text: It expands `*` before the command ever sees it
choices.why: Expansion is the shell's step 3, and a great deal of later confusion comes from forgetting it.

choices.text: It has privileges an ordinary program does not
choices.why: None. What it may do is exactly what your user may do.

prompt: Inside a plain `ubuntu` container, `systemctl status` refuses to do anything and mentions PID 1. What is going on?
hint: Consider how much of a computer a container actually starts.

choices.text: The image is damaged, and pulling it again will restore the missing service manager
choices.why: Every plain distribution image behaves this way. Pulling it again changes nothing.

choices.text: systemd is present but stopped, so it has to be started before anything else works
choices.why: There is nothing to start it. PID 1 is whatever you asked the container to run.

choices.text: The machine did not boot, so the service manager it talks to is not running
choices.why: A container runs a single program rather than a whole system. This is its normal state.

choices.text: You are not root inside this environment, so the request is being refused
choices.why: It is not a permission problem; the message says so. Being root changes nothing here.

prompt: Lesson 5 is about services and systemd. Which practice machine will NOT do for it?

choices.text: A virtual machine
choices.why: It boots like real hardware, so systemd is there in full.

choices.text: A container
choices.why: No boot, so no init system. Use a virtual machine or WSL for that lesson.

choices.text: A rented cloud instance
choices.why: An ordinary booted machine, and the closest thing to how it will be at work.

choices.text: WSL 2
choices.why: A real kernel, and current versions run systemd.

prompt: What does a machine to practise on have to give you? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three properties, and each one rules out something that looks convenient.

choices.text: You can break it without it being a disaster
choices.why: You will run something destructive by accident, and that has to be survivable.

choices.text: You can throw it away and start clean
choices.why: Starting again is a learning tool, not an admission of failure.

choices.text: It is a real Linux, not a simulation of one
choices.why: The whole subject is how the actual system behaves.

choices.text: It has a graphical desktop installed
choices.why: Most machines you will meet professionally have no desktop at all.

choices.text: It is the same distribution as the one used in the videos
choices.why: Lesson 2 is about the differences. Meeting one early is useful rather than a problem.

prompt: Fill the blank: in `docker run -it ___ ubuntu:24.04 bash`, that flag is what deletes the machine the moment you type `exit`.
hint: It is the one that makes the container a throwaway.

prompt: Why is a Mac's Terminal a poor substitute for a Linux on this course, even though most commands work?
hint: It is in the family — the question is what sits above the agreement.

choices.text: It is a BSD userland: flags differ, and `/proc`, `apt` and systemd are absent
choices.why: Fine for lessons 3 and 4, and actively misleading for 2, 5, 7 and 11.

choices.text: macOS sits outside the Unix family, so very little of what you learn here will carry across
choices.why: The opposite: it is a formally registered UNIX. That is why so much does work.

choices.text: Terminal is an emulator rather than a shell, so it runs a simulation of the commands
choices.why: Every terminal is an emulator, including the one on a Linux machine. It runs a real shell.

choices.text: Becoming root on a Mac requires a developer account from Apple
choices.why: `sudo` works there as it does anywhere. That is not the difference.
